timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Hey Stewie, what exactly is DNS?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Peter, DNS is like the phonebook of the internet. When you type google.com, DNS translates it to an IP address like 142.250.80.46.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So it's like when I look up a number in the yellow pages?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly! But here's the thing - if someone poisons that phonebook, they can redirect you to a fake website. You'd think you're logging into your bank, but you're actually sending your credentials to an attacker.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: It is. DNS poisoning is a real and active attack vector. That's why DNSSEC was created - to digitally sign DNS records and prevent tampering.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: DNS filtering is crucial in enterprise environments. Tools like Pi-hole and enterprise DNS servers block malicious domains before they can even be resolved.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Is this something I need to worry about at home?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Absolutely. Use encrypted DNS like DoH (DNS over HTTPS) or DoT (DNS over TLS). Your ISP can see every domain you visit through plain DNS queries.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: The 2016 Dyn attack took down Twitter, Netflix, and Reddit by exploiting DNS infrastructure. One vulnerability, massive impact.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: A common interview question is: explain DNS resolution and how DNS poisoning works. If you can answer that, you're ahead of 90% of candidates.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Now that you understand DNS, let's talk about what happens when those DNS responses travel back to you through HTTP and HTTPS.
